metadata.kicker_note: Fixed series kicker for the claude-hai channel. Not a per-video choice.
metadata.naming_note: Drive naming: the folder carries the identity, the file carries the topic. Delivered as Medhavy_Kehinde/Fact Check/Chapter 1/chapter1.mp4 (16:9) and chapter1-short.mp4 (9:16).
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity skin throughout. Terracotta marks exactly one thing per beat, and on the count beats it marks the rows that did NOT hold up, because those are the point of a review.
metadata.note: PROJECT UPDATE, not an explainer. A straight report on the chapter 1 fact-check: what the work is, what the numbers were, what the failures looked like, what I would carry into chapter 2. Every component used here has a registered 916 portrait variant, so the short derives without a centre cut. All figures are Kehinde's own audit record.

beats.new_visual_element: What arrives in the workbook, and what a reviewer adds
beats.narration: Here is how the work actually arrives. I get an Excel workbook for each chapter, with three tabs. The main tab holds every sentence the AI flagged for a human. There is an AI-only tab it claims needs no review, and an editorial tab for garbled text. For each row I add a decision, a comment with the source link, and the corrected sentence.

beats.new_visual_element: 136 flagged, 105 held up against the source
beats.narration: Chapter one had a hundred and thirty-six rows in the main tab. Every one of them needed a real lookup, against PubMed, the FDA Orange and Purple Books, SEER, the CDC. A hundred and five held up against the source. That is seventy-seven percent.

beats.narration: So here is the split. A hundred and five came back true. Twenty-one were false, and each of those gets a suggested correction with a source link attached. Ten I flagged, which means I could not settle them either way with the sources I had. Those go back with a note, not a guess.

beats.new_visual_element: Two ways a claim fails, and what settles it
beats.narration: And the failures were not all one kind. Some citations were fabricated, a real paper number with invented authors on it. Some numbers were close but wrong, ten to thirty percent where the source said twenty-five to thirty. Some figures were simply old. And some citations were real but did not support the sentence they were attached to.

beats.new_visual_element: What I carry into chapter two
beats.narration: What I would carry out of chapter one. A verdict of true is where the check starts, not where it ends. Nothing counts without a source link sitting in the comment. And I could not settle ten of them, so I said so, rather than guessing and moving on.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the viewer's prompt typed
beats.narration: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take any document that was written or drafted with AI, and pull out ten factual sentences. For each one, write down the exact source you would have to open to confirm it. Then go and open three of them. Tell me which held up, which did not, and which you could not settle. Do not summarise the document. Check it. That last line is the one that matters, because summarising feels like checking, and it is not.
